# Global Navigation and GNSS Measurements {#sec-global-nav} Until now, most of our examples have lived in a friendly local world: a flat plane, a fixed Cartesian reference frame, and distances small enough that Earth's curvature is not the dominant problem. That approximation is useful. It is also limited. For global navigation, the vehicle moves over a rotating, curved Earth, and that changes the inertial bookkeeping in several ways at once. Gravity varies in magnitude with latitude and height, and its direction *defines* "down," which turns as the vehicle moves. A gyro senses Earth's rotation (about $15^\circ$/h) on top of the vehicle's own rotation. The local navigation frame itself rotates as the vehicle travels over the curved surface (the transport rate). Velocity expressed in a rotating frame picks up Coriolis terms. And latitude and longitude are angles, so turning velocity into position requires the Earth's radii of curvature. Get any one of these wrong and the mistake enters the integrators exactly like a sensor bias, growing into attitude, velocity, and position error. For a navigation-grade INS crossing an ocean, every term matters. For the smartphone IMU of Project 3, the gyro bias (hundreds to thousands of degrees per hour) swamps Earth rate, but a wrong gravity sign, a degree-for-radian slip, or a height in the wrong datum is never small. A local flat frame can still be useful, but only as a frame attached to a particular location. If the vehicle moves far enough, the meaning of north, east, and down changes with position. Gravity changes with latitude and height. The Earth rotates under inertial space. A navigation algorithm that ignores those facts will slowly turn geometry into error and then act surprised when the map does not forgive it. This chapter introduces global-scale navigation and the external measurements that will bound inertial drift: satellite radio navigation from a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS). We open the receiver box just far enough to see how four or more pseudoranges become a position and clock estimate, and why satellite geometry sets the quality of that estimate. After that, we treat the receiver mostly as a black box that outputs timestamped position, velocity, and uncertainty. That is enough for loosely coupled INS/GNSS integration, which is the architecture used in the project. The signal-processing and receiver-design details are important, but they are not the focus here. There is an entire branch of PNT (positioning, navigation, and timing) engineering devoted to satellite radio signal processing, and @sec-adv-gnss gives an optional tour of it. Our goal is to understand what a GNSS receiver is estimating, why it needs multiple satellites, why its errors are not simple Gaussian noise, and how its position and velocity outputs become measurements in an INS/GNSS filter. ::: {.callout-note title="Where this sits in the stack"} Guidance and mission logic need a state that is geo-referenced, so that waypoints, charts, and other vehicles share one frame; high-rate, so that control can use it; and always available, so that the vehicle does not go blind under a bridge (@sec-gnc-autonomy-stack). GNSS supplies the first, inertial navigation the second and third, and their integration is how real vehicles deliver all three at once. Because those consumers act on the output without a human checking it, integrity matters as much as accuracy. The navigation system must say when its solution is degraded, which aids it has lost, and how long it has been coasting, and the rest of the stack must have a plan for each of those degraded modes. ::: ## From Local Coordinates to Global Coordinates {#sec-global-nav-from-local-coordinates} The flat-Earth approximation assumes that a local navigation frame can be treated as fixed over the region of interest. For indoor robots, small drones, and many short-range experiments, this is usually acceptable. For aircraft, ships, long-range ground vehicles, and strategic navigation, it is not. Global navigation commonly uses three frames: - **Earth-centered inertial (ECI)**: centered at Earth, but not rotating with Earth. This is the cleanest frame for Newtonian inertial dynamics. - **Earth-centered Earth-fixed (ECEF)**: centered at Earth and rotating with Earth. Coordinates are fixed to the planet, so a point on Earth's surface has constant ECEF coordinates. GNSS satellite positions and receiver fixes are computed here. - **Local navigation frame**: a tangent frame attached to the vehicle. In this course we use North-East-Down (NED), where position is represented by geodetic coordinates (latitude, longitude, and height), and velocity is resolved into northward, eastward, and downward components. The body frame is attached to the vehicle. The IMU measures angular rate and specific force in this body frame. The navigation algorithm must transform those measurements into the navigation frame, integrate the state, and keep track of the fact that the navigation frame itself moves and rotates as the vehicle moves over the ellipsoid. @fig-global-navigation-frames shows the chain and the rotation rate between each link. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-global-navigation-frames %%| fig-cap: "The frame chain for global navigation, labeled with the rotation rate between each pair of frames. A strapdown gyro measures the sum of all three rates, so the mechanization must subtract Earth rate and transport rate to recover the vehicle's rotation relative to the local navigation frame." flowchart LR I["ECI (i)
inertial"] -->|"Earth rate ω_ie
about 15°/h"| E["ECEF (e)
rotates with Earth"] E -->|"transport rate ω_en
about speed / radius"| N["NED (n)
local level, moves with vehicle"] N -->|"vehicle rotation ω_nb"| B["Body (b)
IMU axes, FRD"] ``` Written out, the gyro triad measures $$ \boldsymbol{\omega}_{ib}^b = \mathbf{C}_n^b\left(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n + \boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n\right) + \boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b , $$ and only the last term is the attitude change we want to track. @sec-ins-gnss builds the full mechanization around this decomposition. How far can a flat local frame stretch before it lies? @fig-flat-tangent-wgs84 answers with two numbers. The tangent plane rises above the curved surface by about $d^2/2R$ at a distance $d$ from its origin, and the true local vertical tilts away from the frozen one by $d/R$ radians. The second number is the more dangerous one for an INS. Navigators have known it for centuries: the nautical mile was originally defined as one minute of arc of latitude, so the vertical turns by one arcminute for every nautical mile traveled. An INS that kept a fixed "down" would misproject gravity into the horizontal accelerometer channels by $g \sin(d/R)$, about $0.3$ mg after a single nautical mile. That is a negligible error next to a smartphone accelerometer's bias, and a large one next to a navigation-grade accelerometer's. The transport rate exists to keep "down" pointing down. ::: {#cell-fig-flat-tangent-wgs84 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt R_EARTH_MEAN = 6_371e3 # mean Earth radius [m] distance_m = np.logspace(1, 6.3, 400) # 10 m to 2000 km departure_m = distance_m**2 / (2.0 * R_EARTH_MEAN) tilt_arcmin = np.degrees(distance_m / R_EARTH_MEAN) * 60.0 ARCMIN_TO_MG = 1e3 * np.radians(1.0 / 60.0) # g sin(tilt) in milli-g, small angle landmarks = {"lab": 100.0, "1 nmi": 1852.0, "harbor": 10e3, "coastal leg": 100e3, "ocean leg": 1e6} fig, (ax_h, ax_t) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6)) ax_h.loglog(distance_m, departure_m, color="C0") ax_t.loglog(distance_m, tilt_arcmin, color="C3") for name, d in landmarks.items(): for ax, curve in ((ax_h, d**2 / (2 * R_EARTH_MEAN)), (ax_t, np.degrees(d / R_EARTH_MEAN) * 60)): ax.plot(d, curve, "o", color="0.3", markersize=4) ax.annotate(name, (d, curve), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(-4, 6), ha="right", fontsize=8) ax_h.set_xlabel("distance from frame origin [m]") ax_h.set_ylabel("tangent-plane height above surface [m]") ax_t.set_xlabel("distance from frame origin [m]") ax_t.set_ylabel("tilt of local vertical [arcmin]") secondary = ax_t.secondary_yaxis( "right", functions=(lambda a: a * ARCMIN_TO_MG, lambda m: m / ARCMIN_TO_MG)) secondary.set_ylabel("horizontal gravity error [mg]") for ax in (ax_h, ax_t): ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.25) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![What a frozen flat frame ignores, as a function of distance from its origin (spherical Earth, R = 6371 km). Left: height of the tangent plane above the surface. Right: tilt of the true local vertical relative to the frozen one, and the horizontal gravity error that tilt would create. One nautical mile tilts the vertical by one arcminute.](global-nav_files/figure-html/fig-flat-tangent-wgs84-output-1.png){#fig-flat-tangent-wgs84 width=852 height=332} ::: ::: ### Geodetic coordinates, briefly @sec-frames-earth-frames already develops the machinery we need, so here is only the reminder. Position on the WGS-84 ellipsoid is written as latitude $L$, longitude $\lambda$, and ellipsoidal height $h$, and it maps to ECEF through @eq-frames-geodetic-ecef, $$ \mathbf{r}^e = \begin{bmatrix} (R_N + h)\cos L\cos\lambda \\ (R_N + h)\cos L\sin\lambda \\ \left(R_N(1 - e^2) + h\right)\sin L \end{bmatrix}, $$ with $R_N$ the prime-vertical radius of curvature. The rotation $\mathbf{C}_e^n$ of @eq-frames-cen resolves ECEF vectors in the local NED axes, and the inverse map from ECEF to geodetic coordinates is a short fixed-point iteration. Latitude and longitude are angles, not meters, so small changes must be scaled by the radii of curvature before they behave like distances: $\delta p_N = (R_M + h)\,\delta L$, $\delta p_E = (R_N + h)\cos L\,\delta\lambda$, and $\delta p_D = -\delta h$. A filter state that stores position *errors* in meters next to a nominal state in radians needs that conversion at every boundary. Mixing the two without it is a good way to create a bug that looks like a physics problem. ::: {.callout-warning title="Which height did the receiver give you?"} The navigation equations use ellipsoidal height $h$. Many receivers and phone APIs report height above mean sea level instead, the orthometric height $H \approx h - N_g$, where $N_g$ is the geoid undulation (about $-28$ m in central Massachusetts, and anywhere from roughly $-106$ to $+85$ m worldwide). The NMEA `GGA` sentence reports mean-sea-level altitude with the geoid separation in a separate field. Apple's Core Location `altitude` is above mean sea level (a separate `ellipsoidalAltitude` gives $h$), while Android's `Location.getAltitude()` is above the WGS-84 ellipsoid. Feed $H$ into the filter as $h$ and every fix lands tens of meters too high or too low, while every horizontal plot still looks perfect. Worse, a constant offset is invisible to the innovation tests: the filter simply converges to the wrong height and reports consistent statistics while doing it (Exercise 3). Check the datum of every height field before it touches the state. ::: ## What the GNSS Provides {#sec-global-nav-what-gnss-provides} GNSS is the generic term for satellite navigation systems. Four have global coverage: the Global Positioning System (GPS, United States), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (European Union), and BeiDou (China). Two regional systems augment them: Japan's Quasi-Zenith Satellite System (QZSS), whose inclined, eccentric orbits keep a satellite high over Japan where urban canyons hide low ones, and India's NavIC (formerly IRNSS). A modern receiver, including the one in your phone, tracks several systems at once. A receiver estimates its position and clock offset by listening to radio signals transmitted by satellites whose positions and clock corrections are known from the broadcast navigation message [@kaplanHegarty2017; @misraEnge2006]. Each satellite transmits a time-tagged ranging signal together with a navigation message: its own orbit (the ephemeris), corrections for its onboard atomic clock, health flags, and other parameters the receiver needs. The receiver compares the received signal timing against its own clock. If the satellite clock and receiver clock were perfectly synchronized, signal travel time would give range directly: $$\rho = c(t_r - t_s),$$ where $c$ is the speed of light, $t_s$ is the transmit time, and $t_r$ is the receive time. GPS satellites orbit about 26,560 km from Earth's center, so the travel time is 67 to 86 ms and a timing error of one microsecond is 300 m of range. The receiver clock is an inexpensive quartz oscillator and is never that good, so the measured quantity is a **pseudorange**: $$\tilde{\rho}_s = \left\|\mathbf{r}_s - \mathbf{r}_u\right\| + c\,\delta t_u - c\,\delta t_s + \epsilon_s.$$ {#eq-global-nav-pseudorange} Here $\mathbf{r}_u$ is the receiver antenna position, $\mathbf{r}_s$ is the satellite position at transmit time, $\delta t_u$ is the receiver clock offset, $\delta t_s$ is the satellite clock offset (known from the navigation message), and $\epsilon_s$ collects unmodeled errors such as atmospheric delay, multipath, receiver noise, and residual orbit or clock error. The receiver has four basic unknowns in a standard single-antenna position fix: three position components and its own clock offset. That is why a three-dimensional GNSS solution needs at least four satellites. Each additional constellation adds one more unknown, the offset between that system's time scale and the others, unless the offset is broadcast. More satellites make the solution overdetermined, which lets the receiver average down noise and test for bad measurements when the geometry supports it. ## Solving for Position: Least Squares and DOP {#sec-global-nav-dop-pvt} A receiver's position, velocity, and time (PVT) solution is an estimation problem we already know how to solve. Write the receiver clock offset in meters, $b = c\,\delta t_u$, and assume the satellite clock term of @eq-global-nav-pseudorange has been corrected. The unknown is $\mathbf{x} = [\mathbf{r}_u^T,\ b]^T$ in ECEF, and the model for satellite $s$ is $$ \rho_s(\mathbf{x}) = \left\|\mathbf{r}_s - \mathbf{r}_u\right\| + b . $$ Linearize about a guess $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$. The derivative of the range with respect to the receiver position is minus the unit line-of-sight vector $$ \mathbf{u}_s = \frac{\mathbf{r}_s - \hat{\mathbf{r}}_u}{\left\|\mathbf{r}_s - \hat{\mathbf{r}}_u\right\|}, $$ which points from the receiver to the satellite: moving toward a satellite shortens its range. Stacking all $m$ satellites gives the linearized model $\Delta\boldsymbol{\rho} \approx \mathbf{G}\,\Delta\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}$, with the **geometry matrix** $$ \mathbf{G} = \begin{bmatrix} -\mathbf{u}_1^T & 1 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ -\mathbf{u}_m^T & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Delta\boldsymbol{\rho} = \tilde{\boldsymbol{\rho}} - \boldsymbol{\rho}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}). $$ {#eq-global-nav-geometry-matrix} The least-squares correction is $\Delta\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{G}^T\mathbf{G})^{-1}\mathbf{G}^T\Delta\boldsymbol{\rho}$. Apply it, relinearize, and repeat: this is Gauss-Newton, the same iteration that @sec-ekf-iterated-ekf showed the iterated EKF to be. With unequal measurement variances $\mathbf{R}$, use the weighted form $(\mathbf{G}^T\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{G})^{-1}\mathbf{G}^T\mathbf{R}^{-1}\Delta\boldsymbol{\rho}$. The problem is so mildly nonlinear at satellite distances that a receiver with no idea where it is can start from the center of the Earth and converge in a handful of iterations. The code below builds a synthetic sky over Worcester: satellites placed at chosen azimuths and elevations on a sphere of GPS orbital radius, pseudoranges with a 90 km receiver clock offset and 3 m of noise, and a Gauss-Newton solver that starts at the Earth's center. It uses NumPy only. ::: {#global-nav-pvt-solver .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np C_LIGHT = 299_792_458.0 # speed of light [m/s] WGS84_A = 6_378_137.0 # semi-major axis [m] WGS84_E2 = 6.69437999014e-3 # first eccentricity squared GPS_ORBIT_RADIUS = 26_560e3 # GPS orbit radius from Earth's center [m] def radii(lat: float) -> tuple[float, float]: """Meridian R_M and prime-vertical R_N radii of curvature [m].""" den = 1.0 - WGS84_E2 * np.sin(lat) ** 2 return WGS84_A * (1.0 - WGS84_E2) / den**1.5, WGS84_A / np.sqrt(den) def geodetic_to_ecef(lat: float, lon: float, h: float) -> np.ndarray: """Geodetic (rad, rad, m) to ECEF [m]; the frames chapter derives it.""" R_N = radii(lat)[1] return np.array([(R_N + h) * np.cos(lat) * np.cos(lon), (R_N + h) * np.cos(lat) * np.sin(lon), (R_N * (1.0 - WGS84_E2) + h) * np.sin(lat)]) def C_e_to_n(lat: float, lon: float) -> np.ndarray: """C_e^n: resolve an ECEF vector in local NED axes.""" sL, cL, sl, cl = np.sin(lat), np.cos(lat), np.sin(lon), np.cos(lon) return np.array([[-sL * cl, -sL * sl, cL], [-sl, cl, 0.0], [-cL * cl, -cL * sl, -sL]]) def place_satellites(r_rx, lat, lon, az_deg, el_deg, radius=GPS_ORBIT_RADIUS): """ECEF positions of satellites seen at (azimuth, elevation) from r_rx. Each satellite sits where the line of sight from the receiver meets a sphere of the given orbit radius. """ az, el = np.radians(az_deg), np.radians(el_deg) u_ned = np.column_stack([np.cos(el) * np.cos(az), # north np.cos(el) * np.sin(az), # east -np.sin(el)]) # down (up is negative) u_ecef = u_ned @ C_e_to_n(lat, lon) # rows are (C_n^e u^n)^T b = u_ecef @ r_rx distance = -b + np.sqrt(b**2 - r_rx @ r_rx + radius**2) return r_rx + distance[:, None] * u_ecef def geometry_matrix(sat_ecef: np.ndarray, r_rx: np.ndarray): """Geometry matrix G (rows [-u^T, 1]) and ranges from r_rx to each satellite.""" diff = sat_ecef - r_rx ranges = np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=1) u = diff / ranges[:, None] # unit line of sight, receiver -> satellite return np.column_stack([-u, np.ones(len(ranges))]), ranges def solve_pvt(sat_ecef, pseudoranges, x0=None, max_iter=10, tol_m=1e-4): """Gauss-Newton single-point positioning. Returns the estimate [x, y, z, b] (ECEF meters, clock offset in meters), the geometry matrix at the solution, and the size of each correction step. """ x = np.zeros(4) if x0 is None else np.array(x0, dtype=float) steps = [] for _ in range(max_iter): G, ranges = geometry_matrix(sat_ecef, x[:3]) residual = pseudoranges - (ranges + x[3]) dx = np.linalg.solve(G.T @ G, G.T @ residual) # normal equations x = x + dx steps.append(float(np.linalg.norm(dx))) if steps[-1] < tol_m: break G, _ = geometry_matrix(sat_ecef, x[:3]) return x, G, steps # Truth: a receiver near WPI with a 0.3 ms clock offset (about 90 km of range). lat0, lon0, h0 = np.radians(42.2742), np.radians(-71.8080), 150.0 r_true = geodetic_to_ecef(lat0, lon0, h0) clock_true_m = C_LIGHT * 3.0e-4 sigma_rho = 3.0 # pseudorange noise [m] rng = np.random.default_rng(2024) az_good = np.array([10.0, 60.0, 105.0, 150.0, 200.0, 245.0, 290.0, 330.0]) el_good = np.array([72.0, 28.0, 45.0, 15.0, 60.0, 22.0, 38.0, 12.0]) sats_good = place_satellites(r_true, lat0, lon0, az_good, el_good) rho = (np.linalg.norm(sats_good - r_true, axis=1) + clock_true_m + sigma_rho * rng.standard_normal(len(az_good))) x_hat, G_good, steps = solve_pvt(sats_good, rho) # start at Earth's center err_ned = C_e_to_n(lat0, lon0) @ (x_hat[:3] - r_true) print("satellite ranges [km]:", np.round(np.linalg.norm(sats_good - r_true, axis=1) / 1e3)) print("Gauss-Newton step sizes [m]:", ", ".join(f"{s:.3g}" for s in steps)) print(f"position error NED [m]: {np.round(err_ned, 2)}, " f"clock error: {float(x_hat[3] - clock_true_m):.2f} m") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` satellite ranges [km]: [20435. 22976. 21669. 24173. 20845. 23502. 22166. 24512.] Gauss-Newton step sizes [m]: 7.64e+06, 1.64e+06, 4.45e+04, 28.8, 1.35e-05 position error NED [m]: [-4.34 -1.63 0.87], clock error: 0.66 m ``` ::: ::: Five iterations take the estimate from the center of the Earth to the receiver; the first step alone covers more than 7000 km. The remaining error of a few meters is what 3 m of pseudorange noise buys with this sky. ### Dilution of precision How much does that noise cost in position? If the pseudorange errors are independent with standard deviation $\sigma$, the least-squares covariance is $$ \operatorname{cov}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \sigma^2\,\mathbf{D}, \qquad \mathbf{D} = (\mathbf{G}^T\mathbf{G})^{-1}. $$ The matrix $\mathbf{D}$ depends only on geometry, which makes it a clean way to separate "how good are the measurements" from "how well placed are the satellites." Its diagonal, square-rooted, gives the **dilution of precision** (DOP) factors. Horizontal and vertical only make sense in local axes, so rotate the position block into NED first, $\mathbf{D}^n = \mathbf{C}_e^n\,\mathbf{D}_{rr}\,\mathbf{C}_n^e$: $$ \begin{aligned} \text{GDOP} &= \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{D}}, & \text{PDOP} &= \sqrt{D^n_{NN} + D^n_{EE} + D^n_{DD}}, \\ \text{HDOP} &= \sqrt{D^n_{NN} + D^n_{EE}}, & \text{VDOP} &= \sqrt{D^n_{DD}}, \\ \text{TDOP} &= \sqrt{D_{bb}} . \end{aligned} $$ So the expected horizontal error is roughly $\sigma\cdot\text{HDOP}$, and so on. (An ENU rotation gives the same numbers; only the axis order changes.) The rotation leaves the trace unchanged, so PDOP can be computed in either frame. ::: {#global-nav-dop .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def dop(G: np.ndarray, lat: float, lon: float) -> tuple[dict, np.ndarray]: """DOP factors from an ECEF geometry matrix; also returns the NED cofactor block.""" D = np.linalg.inv(G.T @ G) C = C_e_to_n(lat, lon) D_ned = C @ D[:3, :3] @ C.T factors = { "GDOP": np.sqrt(np.trace(D)), "PDOP": np.sqrt(np.trace(D[:3, :3])), "HDOP": np.sqrt(D_ned[0, 0] + D_ned[1, 1]), "VDOP": np.sqrt(D_ned[2, 2]), "TDOP": np.sqrt(D[3, 3]), } return {k: float(v) for k, v in factors.items()}, D_ned # Poor geometry: six satellites bunched in the north-east quadrant. az_poor = np.array([35.0, 50.0, 62.0, 75.0, 88.0, 100.0]) el_poor = np.array([48.0, 62.0, 35.0, 55.0, 42.0, 66.0]) sats_poor = place_satellites(r_true, lat0, lon0, az_poor, el_poor) def monte_carlo_errors(sats, n_trials=2000): """NED position errors of the PVT solution over repeated noisy epochs.""" true_ranges = np.linalg.norm(sats - r_true, axis=1) x_warm, _, _ = solve_pvt(sats, true_ranges + clock_true_m) # receiver's last fix errors = np.empty((n_trials, 3)) for k in range(n_trials): rho_k = true_ranges + clock_true_m + sigma_rho * rng.standard_normal(len(sats)) x_k, _, _ = solve_pvt(sats, rho_k, x0=x_warm, max_iter=4) errors[k] = C_e_to_n(lat0, lon0) @ (x_k[:3] - r_true) return errors results = {} for name, sats in (("spread", sats_good), ("clustered", sats_poor)): _, G_name, _ = solve_pvt(sats, np.linalg.norm(sats - r_true, axis=1) + clock_true_m) factors, D_ned = dop(G_name, lat0, lon0) errors = monte_carlo_errors(sats) results[name] = (factors, D_ned, errors) rms_h = np.sqrt(np.mean(errors[:, 0] ** 2 + errors[:, 1] ** 2)) rms_v = np.sqrt(np.mean(errors[:, 2] ** 2)) print(f"{name:>9} sky: " + " ".join(f"{k} {v:5.2f}" for k, v in factors.items())) print(f"{'':>15}horizontal RMS {rms_h:6.2f} m (sigma*HDOP {sigma_rho * factors['HDOP']:6.2f} m)," f" vertical RMS {rms_v:6.2f} m (sigma*VDOP {sigma_rho * factors['VDOP']:6.2f} m)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` spread sky: GDOP 1.87 PDOP 1.66 HDOP 0.92 VDOP 1.39 TDOP 0.85 horizontal RMS 2.72 m (sigma*HDOP 2.75 m), vertical RMS 4.07 m (sigma*VDOP 4.16 m) clustered sky: GDOP 25.95 PDOP 18.85 HDOP 11.61 VDOP 14.85 TDOP 17.83 horizontal RMS 35.10 m (sigma*HDOP 34.82 m), vertical RMS 44.70 m (sigma*VDOP 44.55 m) ``` ::: ::: The Monte Carlo errors land on $\sigma\cdot$DOP, as they should for a nearly linear problem with Gaussian noise. The same 3 m pseudoranges give about 3 m of horizontal error from the spread sky and more than 30 m from the clustered one. Nothing about the measurements changed; only where they came from. @fig-global-nav-skyplot shows the two skies, and @fig-global-nav-dop-scatter shows the resulting horizontal errors with the 95% ellipse predicted by $\sigma^2\mathbf{D}^n$. The clustered sky's ellipse is long and thin: the satellites all lie to the north-east, so they pin down position poorly along that direction, and because every line of sight also tilts upward, that weakness is shared with height and the clock. ::: {#cell-fig-global-nav-skyplot .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4), subplot_kw={"projection": "polar"}) for ax, (name, az, el, color) in zip( axes, [("spread", az_good, el_good, "C0"), ("clustered", az_poor, el_poor, "C3")]): ax.set_theta_zero_location("N") ax.set_theta_direction(-1) ax.scatter(np.radians(az), 90.0 - el, s=60, color=color, zorder=3) for i, (a, e) in enumerate(zip(az, el)): ax.annotate(str(i + 1), (np.radians(a), 90.0 - e), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(6, 4), fontsize=8) ax.set_rlim(0, 90) ax.set_rticks([0, 30, 60, 90]) ax.set_yticklabels(["90°", "60°", "30°", "0°"], fontsize=8) ax.set_rlabel_position(157.5) ax.set_title(f"{name} sky: HDOP {results[name][0]['HDOP']:.1f}") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Skyplots (north up, azimuth clockwise, zenith at the center) of the two synthetic skies over Worcester. Both have more than four satellites; only their spread differs.](global-nav_files/figure-html/fig-global-nav-skyplot-output-1.png){#fig-global-nav-skyplot width=758 height=387} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-global-nav-dop-scatter .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} from math import sqrt def ellipse_points(cov2: np.ndarray, scale: float, n: int = 200) -> np.ndarray: """Points on the ellipse x^T cov2^{-1} x = scale^2 (columns: north, east).""" vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov2) t = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0 * np.pi, n) circle = np.vstack([np.cos(t), np.sin(t)]) return (vecs @ (scale * np.sqrt(vals)[:, None] * circle)).T k95 = sqrt(5.991) # chi-square, 2 dof, 95% fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.5)) for ax, name, color, half_width in ((axes[0], "spread", "C0", 12.0), (axes[1], "clustered", "C3", 120.0)): factors, D_ned, errors = results[name] ax.plot(errors[:, 1], errors[:, 0], ".", color=color, alpha=0.25, markersize=3) ell = ellipse_points(sigma_rho**2 * D_ned[:2, :2], k95) ax.plot(ell[:, 1], ell[:, 0], color="k", linewidth=1.5, label="predicted 95%") ax.set_xlim(-half_width, half_width) ax.set_ylim(-half_width, half_width) ax.set_aspect("equal") ax.set_title(f"{name} sky: HDOP {factors['HDOP']:.1f}") ax.set_xlabel("east error [m]") ax.set_ylabel("north error [m]") ax.grid(True, alpha=0.25) ax.legend(loc="upper left") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Horizontal position errors of 2000 single-epoch fixes with 3 m pseudorange noise, and the 95% ellipse predicted from sigma squared times the NED cofactor block. Same noise, different sky; note the tenfold change of scale.](global-nav_files/figure-html/fig-global-nav-dop-scatter-output-1.png){#fig-global-nav-dop-scatter width=854 height=430} ::: ::: Notice also that VDOP exceeds HDOP even for the good sky. All satellites are above the horizon, so the vertical position and the receiver clock push the pseudoranges in similar ways and the least-squares solution struggles to separate them. That is why GNSS height is typically one and a half to two times worse than horizontal position, and why aircraft and survey users care about low-elevation satellites despite their larger atmospheric errors. Two simplifications in this synthetic example deserve a sentence each. A real receiver must account for Earth's rotation during the signal's 70-odd millisecond flight, by rotating each satellite's transmit-time position into the ECEF frame at receive time; this Sagnac correction is worth up to a few tens of meters and is covered in @sec-adv-gnss-tight-coupling. And a real receiver also solves for velocity and clock drift from Doppler measurements with exactly the same geometry matrix, because a range rate is the line-of-sight projection of relative velocity. ### Geometry and Reported Quality DOP is a geometry statement, not an accuracy guarantee. It says nothing by itself about multipath, clock faults, bad atmospheric models, or a measurement that arrived at the wrong time. A receiver commonly summarizes the quality of its solution with satellite count, DOP, an estimated accuracy or covariance, and a fix-type flag. Treat these as evidence to be checked together, not as truth [@groves; @kaplanHegarty2017]. GNSS can also estimate velocity. A receiver uses carrier Doppler (pseudorange rate) to each satellite, which constrains the receiver velocity and clock drift through the same geometry. For our loosely coupled treatment, the receiver output is simply $$\mathbf{z}_{GNSS,k} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{p}_{GNSS,k} \\ \mathbf{v}_{GNSS,k} \end{bmatrix},$$ with a timestamp and some statement of uncertainty. The receiver may report that uncertainty as a covariance matrix, horizontal and vertical accuracy estimates, a DOP value, or a vendor-specific quality flag. In real projects, the exact receiver interface matters. In this course, we will model it as a position (and optionally velocity) measurement with covariance $\mathbf{R}_{GNSS,k}$. ## GNSS Error Sources {#sec-global-nav-gnss-error-sources} GNSS is an external reference, but it is not truth. A receiver solution is an estimate from radio measurements, and radio measurements are sensitive to the environment. @tbl-global-nav-error-budget lists the main pseudorange error sources with representative magnitudes for a single-frequency code receiver; the numbers vary with solar activity, satellite elevation, receiver design, and surroundings, so read them as orders of magnitude [@kaplanHegarty2017; @misraEnge2006]. | Source | Typical size before correction | Typical residual | Character | |---|---|---|---| | Satellite clock and ephemeris | (broadcast values are the correction) | about 0.5 to 1 m | slowly varying, common to all users of a satellite | | Ionosphere | 1 to 15 m at zenith, several times more at low elevation or high solar activity | roughly half removed by the broadcast model; first order removed by dual-frequency | dispersive, varies with time of day and latitude | | Troposphere | about 2.4 m at zenith, about 25 m at 5° elevation | about 0.1 to 0.5 m with a standard model | non-dispersive, mostly predictable | | Multipath | 0.5 to a few m in open sky; tens of m in urban canyons | not removed by models | environment dependent, time-correlated | | Receiver noise | 0.1 to 1 m for code; millimeters for carrier phase | not removed by models | nearly white, grows as signal strength falls | : Representative pseudorange error budget for a single-frequency code receiver. Combined with HDOP, a user equivalent range error of a few meters explains the familiar few-meter open-sky phone fix. {#tbl-global-nav-error-budget} Several further error mechanisms do not fit neatly into a per-satellite budget. Non-line-of-sight reception happens when the direct signal is blocked and only a reflection arrives, which adds a positive range error that can be tens of meters and is not bounded the way multipath is. Outages and obstructions, from tunnels, indoor spaces, dense urban corridors, foliage, and the vehicle body itself, remove satellites and degrade geometry. Timing and synchronization errors are self-inflicted: a GNSS measurement must be compared against the INS state at the same time of validity, and a 100 ms mismatch at highway speed is a 3 m error before any radio physics enters. These errors are not all independent, zero-mean, or white. Multipath and atmospheric residuals are time-correlated over seconds to hours. Receiver filtering can smooth noise but lengthens its correlation time. Satellite geometry changes slowly. A high-rate GNSS output does not automatically mean that every sample contains independent information. That point matters for Kalman filtering. If $\mathbf{R}_{GNSS}$ is too small, the filter will believe GNSS too aggressively and may inject jumps or multipath errors into the inertial solution. If $\mathbf{R}_{GNSS}$ is too large, the filter will fail to correct INS drift quickly enough. A practical implementation should adapt or gate GNSS measurements using receiver quality flags, innovation size, reported accuracy, satellite count, geometry, and knowledge of the operating environment, and check the result with the consistency tools of @sec-kf-consistency. ### Jamming and Spoofing GNSS signals arrive at the antenna at roughly $-128$ dBm, about $10^{-16}$ W, which is below the thermal noise floor of the receiver's bandwidth; the receiver digs them out only because it knows the spreading code. That makes the whole system easy to drown. A jammer of a few watts can deny GNSS over tens of kilometers on the ground, and much farther to an aircraft with line of sight. A spoofer is more insidious: it broadcasts counterfeit signals that the receiver accepts, so the output is a confident, smoothly moving, wrong position. These are operational realities, not thought experiments. Ships in the Black Sea reported GPS positions placing them inland in 2017, and later analysis documented systematic spoofing around sensitive sites [@c4ads2019]. Since 2023, airliners over parts of the Middle East have been spoofed in large numbers, and flights around the Baltic have met persistent jamming and, increasingly, spoofing, prompting aviation-safety bulletins and changes to operating procedures [@easaSib202202]. Every robot that leaves the lab with a GNSS receiver should be designed on the assumption that GNSS will sometimes be absent or lying. An INS is the natural detector and fallback: a spoofed position must also agree with what the inertial sensors felt, and the innovation tests of an integrated filter are the first line of defense. @sec-adv-gnss-raim develops receiver autonomous integrity monitoring, the classic residual test, and the cues receivers use to recognize interference. ### Accuracy, Availability, and Integrity **Accuracy** is closeness to the true state. **Availability** is whether a service or measurement is usable under its declared conditions. **Integrity** is the ability to warn when the system should not be used as intended. A small reported standard deviation is an accuracy statement; it is not an integrity guarantee. For the project, record quality flags, use innovation gating, and make stale or rejected measurements visible in diagnostics. ## Why INS and GNSS Fit Together {#sec-global-nav-why-ins-gnss} An inertial navigation system and a GNSS receiver fail in different ways. That is why they are useful together. | Sensor | Strength | Weakness | |------------------------|------------------------|------------------------| | INS / IMU | high-rate, smooth, self-contained, immune to jamming | drifts over time because biases and noise are integrated | | GNSS | globally referenced position and velocity with bounded error | lower rate, noisier short term, vulnerable to obstruction, interference, and spoofing | INS gives the filter a high-rate propagation model. GNSS gives the filter an external correction. During a short GNSS outage, the INS can coast while its uncertainty grows; when GNSS returns, it pulls the inertial solution back toward the global reference frame (@fig-gnss-outage-ins-drift). The system is not magic; it is a trade between short-term continuity and long-term bounded error. How long the coast can last depends on the IMU grade: a navigation-grade unit drifts on the order of a nautical mile per hour, while a smartphone IMU can be a kilometer off within about a minute. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-gnss-outage-ins-drift %%| fig-cap: "GNSS bounds long-term inertial drift; uncertainty must grow during an aiding outage." sequenceDiagram participant INS as INS propagation participant GNSS as GNSS update GNSS->>INS: position and velocity correction Note over INS,GNSS: bounded uncertainty Note over INS: GNSS outage: propagate only Note over INS: covariance grows GNSS->>INS: timestamped recovery update ``` ## Loosely Coupled INS/GNSS Integration {#sec-global-nav-loosely-coupled-ins} In a loosely coupled architecture, the GNSS receiver computes its own navigation solution first. The INS/GNSS filter then uses that receiver solution as a measurement. The filter does not process raw satellite pseudoranges or carrier-phase observables. This is the architecture we will use (@fig-loose-ins-gnss-architecture): 1. The IMU drives high-rate strapdown propagation. 2. The GNSS receiver outputs timestamped position and velocity. 3. The filter forms a GNSS-minus-INS innovation. 4. The Kalman update estimates the INS error state. 5. The estimated error is injected back into the nominal navigation state. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-loose-ins-gnss-architecture %%| fig-cap: "Loose INS/GNSS integration uses receiver position and velocity as measurements of a propagated nominal state." flowchart LR IMU["IMU samples"] --> PROP["Strapdown nominal propagation"] GNSS["GNSS PVT: position, velocity, quality"] --> UPDATE["Error-state measurement update"] PROP --> UPDATE UPDATE --> INJECT["Inject state and bias correction"] INJECT --> PROP ``` The nominal inertial state is $$\mathbf{x}_{nom} = \left[ L,\ \lambda,\ h,\ \mathbf{v}^n,\ \mathbf{q}_b^n,\ \mathbf{b}_a,\ \mathbf{b}_g \right],$$ geodetic position, NED velocity, attitude, and the accelerometer and gyroscope biases. The error-state filter estimates small corrections $$\delta \mathbf{x} = \left[ \delta \mathbf{p},\ \delta \mathbf{v},\ \delta \boldsymbol{\theta},\ \delta \mathbf{b}_a,\ \delta \mathbf{b}_g \right]^T,$$ where, unlike the nominal position, the position error $\delta\mathbf{p}$ is in NED meters (@sec-ins-gnss-error-state-formulation). ### The position innovation and the lever arm That mismatch of units is where the first real bug usually hides. The receiver reports the antenna's latitude, longitude, and height; the INS carries the IMU's. Before anything can be subtracted, the GNSS fix is converted into NED meters relative to the current nominal position $(\hat{L}, \hat{\lambda}, \hat{h})$: $$ \mathbf{z}_k = \begin{bmatrix} (R_M + \hat{h})(L_{GNSS} - \hat{L}) \\ (R_N + \hat{h})\cos\hat{L}\,(\lambda_{GNSS} - \hat{\lambda}) \\ -(h_{GNSS} - \hat{h}) \end{bmatrix}. $$ {#eq-global-nav-gnss-ned-offset} If the GNSS antenna is not at the IMU, the receiver measures a different point. With $\boldsymbol{\ell}^b$ the vector from the IMU to the antenna in body axes, the antenna sits at $\mathbf{C}_b^n\boldsymbol{\ell}^b$ meters from the IMU in NED, so the predicted measurement is $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_k = \hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\boldsymbol{\ell}^b$ and the innovation is $$ \boldsymbol{\nu}_k = \mathbf{z}_k - \hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\boldsymbol{\ell}^b . $$ The tempting shortcut, adding $\mathbf{C}_b^n\boldsymbol{\ell}^b$ directly to $(L, \lambda, h)$, adds meters to radians; the conversion runs the other way with $\delta L = \delta p_N/(R_M + h)$, $\delta\lambda = \delta p_E/((R_N + h)\cos L)$, and $\delta h = -\delta p_D$. Because the lever-arm term depends on attitude, the measurement Jacobian gains an attitude block, $$ \mathbf{H}_k = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{I}_3 & \mathbf{0}_3 & -\left[\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\boldsymbol{\ell}^b\right]_\times & \mathbf{0}_3 & \mathbf{0}_3 \end{bmatrix}, $$ derived in @sec-ins-gnss-loose-gnss-measurement. Do not ignore the lever arm just because it is inconvenient. On a small ground robot it may be negligible. On a ship with the antenna at the masthead, every roll swings the antenna meters sideways (Exercise 4), and an ignored lever arm turns that motion into a self-inflicted residual. The same term is also a gift: it makes attitude errors visible in position measurements whenever the vehicle rotates. Velocity works the same way. The antenna velocity adds the lever arm's rotational motion, $\mathbf{C}_b^n(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b\times\boldsymbol{\ell}^b)$, and the velocity rows of $\mathbf{H}$ select $\delta\mathbf{v}$ (@sec-ins-gnss-lever-arm-timing). A phone that reports only speed and course gives horizontal velocity only, so use two rows, not three. Some texts define the innovation as INS-minus-GNSS and flip the signs in $\mathbf{H}$; either works if used consistently, and this course uses GNSS-minus-INS with errors defined as true minus estimate. The code below implements @eq-global-nav-gnss-ned-offset and the lever-arm innovation, then checks both against an exact ECEF computation: a "true" IMU displaced from the nominal one by a known $\delta\mathbf{p}$, rotated by a known $\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}$, carrying an antenna on a 2 m mast. ::: {#global-nav-loose-update .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} def skew(a: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """[a]_x such that skew(a) @ b == np.cross(a, b).""" return np.array([[0.0, -a[2], a[1]], [a[2], 0.0, -a[0]], [-a[1], a[0], 0.0]]) def rotvec_to_dcm(phi: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """Rotation matrix of a rotation vector (Rodrigues formula).""" angle = np.linalg.norm(phi) if angle < 1e-12: return np.eye(3) + skew(phi) K = skew(phi / angle) return np.eye(3) + np.sin(angle) * K + (1.0 - np.cos(angle)) * K @ K def ecef_to_geodetic(r_e: np.ndarray) -> tuple[float, float, float]: """ECEF [m] to geodetic (rad, rad, m) by fixed-point iteration on latitude.""" x, y, z = r_e p = np.hypot(x, y) lat = np.arctan2(z, p * (1.0 - WGS84_E2)) for _ in range(10): lat = np.arctan2(z + WGS84_E2 * radii(lat)[1] * np.sin(lat), p) h = p * np.cos(lat) + z * np.sin(lat) - WGS84_A**2 / radii(lat)[1] return lat, np.arctan2(y, x), h def gnss_position_innovation(nominal, C_bn_hat, lever_arm_b, fix): """Loose GNSS position innovation and Jacobian for the 15-state error vector. nominal, fix: (lat, lon, h) in rad, rad, m. Returns nu (NED meters) and H (3x15). """ lat, lon, h = nominal R_M, R_N = radii(lat) z = np.array([(R_M + h) * (fix[0] - lat), # GNSS fix in NED meters (R_N + h) * np.cos(lat) * (fix[1] - lon), # relative to the nominal -(fix[2] - h)]) # IMU position lever_n = C_bn_hat @ lever_arm_b nu = z - lever_n H = np.zeros((3, 15)) H[:, 0:3] = np.eye(3) H[:, 6:9] = -skew(lever_n) # attitude block return nu, H def ned_to_geodetic_correction(dp_ned, lat, h): """Convert an NED-meter position correction into (dL, dlambda, dh).""" R_M, R_N = radii(lat) return np.array([dp_ned[0] / (R_M + h), dp_ned[1] / ((R_N + h) * np.cos(lat)), -dp_ned[2]]) def loose_gnss_update(P, nu, H, R): """Error-state Kalman update (Joseph form). Returns delta_x_hat and P_{k|k}.""" S = H @ P @ H.T + R K = np.linalg.solve(S, H @ P).T # P H^T S^{-1} without an inverse delta_x = K @ nu # error-state prior mean is zero I_KH = np.eye(P.shape[0]) - K @ H return delta_x, I_KH @ P @ I_KH.T + K @ R @ K.T # Nominal state, and a known error: dp = (4, -3, 1.5) m NED, dtheta = (2, -1, 3) deg. nominal = (lat0, lon0, h0) C_bn_hat = rotvec_to_dcm(np.radians([0.0, 4.0, 30.0])) # some nominal attitude lever_arm_b = np.array([0.5, 0.0, -2.0]) # antenna 2 m above the IMU (FRD) dp_true = np.array([4.0, -3.0, 1.5]) dtheta_true = np.radians([2.0, -1.0, 3.0]) # Exact truth through ECEF: true IMU position, true attitude, true antenna position. r_imu = geodetic_to_ecef(*nominal) + C_e_to_n(lat0, lon0).T @ dp_true C_bn_true = rotvec_to_dcm(dtheta_true) @ C_bn_hat # C = (I + [dtheta]x) C_hat to 1st order r_ant = r_imu + C_e_to_n(lat0, lon0).T @ (C_bn_true @ lever_arm_b) fix = ecef_to_geodetic(r_ant) nu, H = gnss_position_innovation(nominal, C_bn_hat, lever_arm_b, fix) delta_x_true = np.concatenate([dp_true, np.zeros(3), dtheta_true, np.zeros(6)]) print("innovation nu [m]: ", np.round(nu, 4)) print("H @ delta_x (linear model): ", np.round(H @ delta_x_true, 4)) print(f"linearization error: {1e3 * np.linalg.norm(nu - H @ delta_x_true):.1f} mm") # One update from a 10 m / 5 deg prior with a 3 m (horizontal) / 5 m (vertical) fix. P = np.diag(np.r_[np.full(3, 10.0**2), np.full(3, 1.0**2), np.full(3, np.radians(5.0)**2), np.full(3, 0.1**2), np.full(3, np.radians(0.1)**2)]) R = np.diag([3.0**2, 3.0**2, 5.0**2]) delta_x_hat, P_post = loose_gnss_update(P, nu, H, R) d_geo = ned_to_geodetic_correction(delta_x_hat[:3], lat0, h0) print("position correction [m]: ", np.round(delta_x_hat[:3], 2)) print(f"as (dL, dlambda) [arcsec]: ({np.degrees(d_geo[0]) * 3600:.4f}, " f"{np.degrees(d_geo[1]) * 3600:.4f}), dh {d_geo[2]:.2f} m") assert np.allclose(P_post, P_post.T) and np.all(np.linalg.eigvalsh(P_post) > 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` innovation nu [m]: [ 4.0218 -2.9132 1.5144] H @ delta_x (linear model): [ 4.0242 -2.9136 1.5127] linearization error: 3.0 mm position correction [m]: [ 3.69 -2.67 1.21] as (dL, dlambda) [arcsec]: (0.1195, -0.1166), dh -1.21 m ``` ::: ::: The linearized model reproduces the exact ECEF innovation to within a few millimeters, the size of the second-order attitude terms over a 2 m lever arm. The code above is not a complete INS/GNSS system. It is the measurement-update shape. A complete implementation also needs strapdown propagation, error-state propagation, measurement gating, timestamp handling, error injection, and error-state reset, which @sec-ins-gnss assembles. ## Loose, Tight, and Deep Coupling {#sec-global-nav-loose-tight-deep} The coupling terms describe where GNSS information enters the integrated navigation algorithm [@groves]. They are a statement about architecture, robustness, and integrity, not about accuracy. **Loosely coupled** integration works in the position domain: the receiver computes its own PVT solution, and the integration filter treats that solution as a measurement. It is modular and straightforward to validate, which is why the project uses it. It has two structural weaknesses. It needs a receiver fix, normally four or more satellites, so it gets nothing from the two or three satellites visible in an urban canyon. And the receiver's own navigation filter makes its output errors time-correlated, so a second Kalman filter that treats them as white noise becomes overconfident; this is the cascaded-filter problem, and it is managed by inflating $\mathbf{R}_{GNSS}$ or reducing the update rate. **Tightly coupled** integration works in the range domain: the filter processes each satellite's pseudorange and pseudorange rate directly and carries the receiver clock bias and drift as extra states. The benefits follow from that. It keeps aiding the INS with fewer than four satellites, because the inertial prediction supplies the missing geometry and each pseudorange still constrains position along its own line of sight. It can test each satellite's residual against the INS prediction and exclude a faulty one, which is per-satellite fault detection and exclusion. And it avoids the cascaded filters, so the measurement errors are closer to the white noise the Kalman filter assumes. The price is a more detailed model: satellite positions, clocks, atmosphere, Earth rotation, and receiver clock dynamics all become the integrator's problem. **Deeply coupled** (or ultra-tight) integration goes inside the receiver: the INS-predicted line-of-sight dynamics aid, or replace, the receiver's code and carrier tracking loops. Because the INS removes the vehicle's motion from what the loops must follow, the loops can use narrower bandwidths. That buys tracking at lower carrier-to-noise ratios, tracking through higher dynamics, faster reacquisition after an outage, and better resistance to jamming. This is receiver-design territory and is outside this course's implementation scope. Centimeter-level accuracy comes from a different axis entirely: carrier-phase processing, such as real-time kinematic (RTK) or precise point positioning (PPP), with its integer ambiguities and correction streams (@sec-adv-gnss-carrier-phase-corrections). A carrier-phase solution can feed a loosely coupled filter as an RTK position fix, or its observables can enter a tightly coupled one. Either way, the centimeters come from the carrier, and the coupling determines how gracefully the system degrades when satellites disappear or misbehave. For this course, tight and deep coupling are comparison points only. They are worth knowing because they explain why professional GNSS/INS systems look more complicated than the filter we implement here, and @sec-adv-gnss-tight-coupling works through the tightly coupled measurement model for readers who want it. They are not required for the assignment. ## Practical Checklist for the Project {#sec-global-nav-practical-checklist-project} When using GNSS measurements in the INS/GNSS project, check the following: - Confirm the coordinate frame of the GNSS position and velocity. - Confirm whether the height is ellipsoidal or mean sea level, and convert to ellipsoidal height before it touches the state. - Convert latitude and longitude differences to NED meters before filtering (@eq-global-nav-gnss-ned-offset), and convert corrections back before injecting them. - Use the GNSS timestamp, not the time at which your code happened to process the message. - Account for the IMU-to-antenna lever arm when it is non-negligible, including its attitude block in $\mathbf{H}$. - Gate large innovations before letting them update the filter. - Choose $\mathbf{R}_{GNSS}$ from reported uncertainty when available; otherwise choose conservative values and tune using innovation statistics. - Treat outages explicitly. Do not feed stale GNSS measurements as if they were current. @sec-ins-gnss develops the curved-Earth strapdown equations used for INS propagation. After that, @sec-ins-errors explains why the error-state model needs bias and noise states. Together, those pieces give us the loose INS/GNSS system used in the final project. ## Exercises {#sec-global-nav-exercises} 1. **DOP by hand, then by code.** One satellite is at the zenith and three are at elevation $30^\circ$, spaced $120^\circ$ apart in azimuth. Then apply a $15^\circ$ elevation mask instead of weighting. Where does the filter's height estimate converge, and will the NIS test flag the problem? (b) How large is the resulting gravity error from the free-air gradient (about $3.1\ \mu$m/s² per meter), and does it matter for a smartphone IMU? (c) Halfway through a run, the logger switches to a source that reports ellipsoidal height.
